The nuclear shape of this particular cell is closer to a band neutrophil or monocyte than to a segmented neutrophil. Background red cells show refractile drying artifact without parasites. In a patient with metastatic melanoma, findings are consistent with phagocytosed melanin pigment in circulating phagocytes (melanin-laden leukocytes); a Fontana-Masson stain can confirm melanin.

title: Metastatic Neuroblastoma - 6.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy (H&E) shows a central aggregate of intermediate-sized cells with round to oval nuclei, finely dispersed pale chromatin, and scant ill-defined cytoplasm, with mitotic figures, surrounded by residual granulocytic and eosinophilic hematopoiesis. Homer Wright rosettes and fibrillary neuropil are not identified, so on morphology alone the infiltrate cannot be distinguished from a hematolymphoid blast population. Immunohistochemistry (PHOX2B, synaptophysin, chromogranin, with negative CD45/TdT) and urine catecholamines are required. With that support, the infiltrate is compatible with metastatic neuroblastoma.

title: Herpes Zoster Lymphadenitis - 2.
describe_en: Lymph node section shows a polymorphous infiltrate composed of small lymphocytes, numerous medium to large activated lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli, and admixed epithelioid histiocytes. A few cells have cleared, glassy-appearing nuclei suggestive of possible viral cytopathic change, although definite Cowdry A inclusions or multinucleation cannot be confirmed at this resolution. There are no monotonous sheets of atypical cells. The appearance is that of an atypical reactive immunoblastic lymphadenitis compatible with herpes zoster lymphadenitis in the right clinical setting; VZV immunohistochemistry or PCR is needed for confirmation.

title: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a mature-appearing monocyte with abundant grey-blue cytoplasm and a folded, reniform nucleus with lacy chromatin, accompanied by two segmented neutrophils. Red cells show mild anisocytosis with occasional target cells and an echinocyte, and platelets are present in small numbers. No blasts are seen in this field. A single monocyte is nonspecific, but an absolute monocytosis in a young child is a required criterion for juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and should prompt a full differential count and molecular evaluation.

title: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 5.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows marked anisopoikilocytosis with ovalocytes, occasional teardrop cells, small fragmented forms and an echinocyte, with variable central pallor. No leukocytes or platelets are included in this field, so the white cell and platelet findings that define juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia cannot be assessed. The red cell changes are nonspecific; they may be seen in JMML, but the diagnosis requires monocytosis, circulating immature myeloid and nucleated red cells, and supporting laboratory and genetic findings.

title: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 6.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear at high power shows red cells with mild anisocytosis and scattered small nucleated cells with dense chromatin and scant cytoplasm, most suggestive of nucleated red blood cells or small lymphocytes; cytoplasmic detail is insufficient to separate them with confidence. Platelets are sparse. No monocytes or blasts are present in this field. These findings are nonspecific but can be seen in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, where circulating nucleated red cells and thrombocytopenia accompany monocytosis.

title: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 7.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows two eosinophils with bilobed nuclei and coarse cytoplasmic granules, a small mature lymphocyte, and red cells with mild anisopoikilocytosis. Monocytosis, circulating myeloid precursors, blasts, and nucleated red cells are not seen in this limited field. The eosinophilia is a non-specific finding. Diagnosis of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia requires an absolute monocyte count of at least 1 x10^9/L, splenomegaly, and a RAS-pathway mutation (PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, CBL, or NF1), which cannot be established from this image.

title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis - 2.
describe_en: Section at low to intermediate power shows sheets of cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and well-defined borders, admixed with numerous eosinophils, and a central aggregate of small lymphocytes containing a few larger cells. Nuclear detail, including the characteristic grooved or coffee-bean nuclei, cannot be assessed at this magnification. Necrosis or eosinophilic abscesses are not clearly seen in this field. Findings are suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis; confirmation requires immunohistochemistry for CD1a, langerin (CD207), and S100, and BRAF V600E testing is recommended.

title: Dysplastic Erythroid Precursor - 1.
describe_en: Smear at high power shows a large early erythroid precursor, consistent with a proerythroblast or basophilic normoblast, with a round nucleus, finely stippled chromatin and intensely basophilic cytoplasm bearing an irregular cytoplasmic bleb. Definite dysplastic features such as nuclear budding, multinuclearity, internuclear bridging or megaloblastoid asynchrony are not clearly demonstrated in this single cell. The background shows a stippled artifact. The image fits an early erythroid precursor, but dyserythropoiesis cannot be firmly established from this field alone.

title: Refractory Anemia with Excess Blasts - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at high power shows a blast with a large round nucleus, finely dispersed chromatin and scant agranular basophilic cytoplasm, surrounded by basophilic erythroid precursors, myelocytes and orthochromatic normoblasts. No Auer rods are identified. Definite dysplastic features are not conspicuous in this single field, and the blast percentage cannot be derived from it. In the context of cytopenias and a 500-cell differential showing 5-19% blasts, findings would be consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts.

title: Hypocellular MDS - 3.
describe_en: Low-power view of a bone marrow aspirate particle shows a predominance of large adipocyte spaces with hematopoietic cells sparsely distributed along intervening stromal strands. Central areas are densely stained, likely representing stroma and crushed cells. Individual cell morphology cannot be evaluated at this magnification, so dysplasia and blast percentage cannot be assessed. The particle appears hypocellular, but aspirate particles are an imperfect surrogate for cellularity, which should be determined on an adequate core biopsy. Findings are compatible with a hypocellular marrow, which in the stated context supports but does not establish hypocellular myelodysplastic neoplasm.

title: Hypocellular MDS - 4.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows trilineage precursors with erythroid and granulocytic elements at multiple stages of maturation. Several basophilic erythroblasts show relatively fine chromatin and deeply basophilic cytoplasm, raising the possibility of mild megaloblastoid dyserythropoiesis, and an early proerythroblast-like cell with a visible nucleolus is present. Granulocytic precursors appear normally granulated, and blasts are not obviously increased in this field. Dysplasia is subtle here, and marrow cellularity cannot be assessed from the aspirate; correlation with the core biopsy (age-adjusted cellularity), dysplasia quantification across 200 cells, and cytogenetics is required to support hypocellular myelodysplastic neoplasm.

title: Hypocellular MDS - 6.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows erythroid and granulocytic precursors in a background of red cells. Erythroid dysplasia is evident, including a binucleated erythroid precursor and another precursor with an irregular, lobulated nucleus, together with large basophilic erythroblasts showing fine chromatin. Granulocytic precursors appear appropriately granulated, and blasts are not increased in this field. These dyserythropoietic changes are nonspecific in isolation; at least 10% dysplastic erythroid cells, correlation with a hypocellular core biopsy, exclusion of nutritional and toxic causes, and cytogenetics are needed to support hypocellular myelodysplastic neoplasm.

title: Prolymphocytic Leukemia - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows two intermediate-sized lymphoid cells with round nuclei, moderately condensed chromatin and a moderate amount of pale blue agranular cytoplasm. A single prominent central nucleolus, characteristic of prolymphocytes, is not clearly resolved in this image. The cells are more mature-appearing than lymphoblasts. Findings are suggestive of a mature lymphoid neoplasm with prolymphocytoid cells; flow cytometry and cytogenetics are required to distinguish B-PLL, T-PLL, CLL with increased prolymphocytes and mantle cell lymphoma. The archive category of B-lymphoblastic leukemia does not match this morphology.

title: Refractory Anemia with Ring Sideroblasts - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows a cluster of basophilic and early polychromatic erythroid precursors with round nuclei, relatively fine chromatin, and deeply basophilic cytoplasm, suggestive of mild megaloblastoid dyserythropoiesis. Accompanying granulocytic precursors, including a band neutrophil and myelocytes, show no obvious dysplasia in this field. No iron stain is provided, so ring sideroblasts cannot be evaluated here. The findings are compatible with, but not diagnostic of, myelodysplastic neoplasm with ring sideroblasts; a Prussian blue stain to quantify ring sideroblasts and SF3B1 mutation testing are required.

title: Refractory Anemia with Ring Sideroblasts - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows erythroid predominance with precursors at all stages of maturation. Several erythroid precursors show dysplastic features, including binucleation, nuclear lobation and notching, and megaloblastoid chromatin in large basophilic erythroblasts. Granulocytic precursors are present in small numbers, and blasts are not increased in this field. Findings indicate dyserythropoiesis consistent with myelodysplastic neoplasm with ring sideroblasts in the stated context; however, ring sideroblasts must be demonstrated and counted on a Prussian blue stain, and SF3B1 status determined.

title: Basophilic Stippling - Lead Poisoning - 4.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows mild anisopoikilocytosis with scattered folded and stomatocyte-like red cells. A central erythrocyte contains several coarse, dark blue-purple granules; they are clustered along one margin rather than distributed evenly throughout the cell, and only faint fine stippling is seen in occasional other cells. The findings are compatible with coarse basophilic stippling as labeled (as seen in lead poisoning), but the peripheral clustering also raises Pappenheimer bodies, which a Prussian blue stain would distinguish. Correlation with blood lead and zinc protoporphyrin levels is recommended.

title: Iron Stain - 1.
describe_en: Prussian blue-stained bone marrow aspirate smear shows a large marrow particle diffusely and densely laden with coarse, confluent blue-green hemosiderin, set against orange-brown red cells. Storage iron is markedly increased (approximately grade 4+ to 5+ in this field). Individual macrophages and erythroid precursors cannot be evaluated for sideroblasts in this thick, slightly out-of-focus particle. These findings exclude iron deficiency and indicate abundant storage iron, as seen in iron overload, anemia of inflammation, or ineffective erythropoiesis; thin areas should be examined for ring sideroblasts.

title: Iron Stain - 2.
describe_en: Prussian blue-stained bone marrow aspirate smear shows a marrow particle with abundant blue granular and diffuse hemosiderin deposits within stromal macrophages, against an orange-brown red cell background. Storage iron appears present and at least adequate to increased (approximately grade 3-4+ on this field). Erythroid precursors cannot be evaluated for sideroblasts in this thick particle. These findings do not support iron deficiency; if the clinical question is iron deficiency, abundant stainable iron would instead point toward anemia of inflammation, iron overload, or ineffective erythropoiesis.

title: Micromegakaryocyte - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows a megakaryocyte with a single, non-lobated, eccentrically placed round nucleus and abundant finely granular cytoplasm, set in a background rich in maturing granulocytes including bands, segmented neutrophils, and metamyelocytes. The cell is clearly larger than the surrounding granulocytes and therefore exceeds the size usually used to define a true micromegakaryocyte (at or below the size of a promyelocyte). It is better described as a small hypolobated (mononuclear) megakaryocyte. Only one megakaryocyte is present, so the proportion of dysplastic forms cannot be assessed; a count across the aspirate and biopsy is needed before attributing this to a reactive versus myelodysplastic process.

title: Anemia and thrombocytopenia: diagnosis from the blood smear
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows normocytic red cells with scattered polychromatic cells and a paucity of platelets. A reactive-appearing lymphocyte is present (A). Several erythrocytes contain small, dark, punctate to ring-like inclusions, and similar tiny blue bodies are seen extracellularly (B); pigment, Schüffner dots, gametocytes and tetrad (Maltese cross) forms cannot be confidently assessed at this resolution. Findings are suggestive of an intraerythrocytic parasitic infection such as babesiosis in the appropriate epidemiologic context; confirmation by thick and thin film review at high magnification, parasitemia estimation and PCR is required.

title: Pelger-Huet Anomoly - 6.
describe_en: Very low-power view of a peripheral blood smear shows an evenly spread monolayer of red cells with a few scattered leukocytes. The leukocyte nuclei appear compact and dense, but nuclear lobation, chromatin pattern, and cytoplasmic granulation cannot be evaluated at this magnification. This field is useful for choosing an area for high-power review rather than for diagnosis. Findings are nonspecific; Pelger-Huët anomaly requires high-power demonstration of bilobed or non-segmented neutrophils with mature chromatin across the neutrophil population.

title: NK Cell Lymphocytosis - 2.
describe_en: Low-power view of a peripheral blood smear shows normochromic, normocytic red cells with adequate platelets. A single medium-sized lymphocyte with condensed chromatin and a moderate rim of pale blue cytoplasm is present centrally; cytoplasmic azurophilic granules cannot be resolved at this magnification. No blasts or atypical nucleolated cells are seen in this field. The image is compatible with a large granular lymphocyte in the setting of NK-cell lymphocytosis, but quantification and granule assessment require higher power and an absolute count, with flow cytometry to confirm NK phenotype.

title: NK Cell Lymphocytosis - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear at intermediate power shows several lymphocytes with abundant pale blue cytoplasm and mature condensed chromatin, clustered with segmented and band neutrophils. One lymphoid cell has faintly granular pinkish cytoplasm, but discrete azurophilic granules are not well resolved at this magnification. No blasts or atypical nucleolated cells are identified. The appearance is compatible with increased large granular lymphocytes in NK-cell lymphocytosis; confirmation requires an absolute LGL count and flow cytometric immunophenotyping.

title: NK Cell Lymphocytosis - 7.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a cluster of lymphocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and mature condensed chromatin, accompanied by segmented and band neutrophils and a small mature lymphocyte. Granularity of the lymphoid cytoplasm is not clearly resolved at this magnification. There are no blasts or overtly atypical cells in the field. Findings are suggestive of large granular lymphocytes in the context of NK-cell lymphocytosis, with high-power review, absolute counts and flow cytometry needed for confirmation.

title: Granular ALL - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows circulating intermediate-sized blasts with round nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli and a narrow rim of pale blue cytoplasm. A mature small lymphocyte and a nucleated red blood cell are present for size comparison. Cytoplasmic azurophilic granules, which define granular ALL, are not clearly resolved at this magnification, and Auer rods are absent. Findings are consistent with circulating blasts compatible with acute lymphoblastic leukemia; MPO cytochemistry and flow cytometry are necessary, particularly to exclude AML in a granular blast population.

title: Granular ALL - 10.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear at high power shows a single blast with a very high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, a slightly indented nucleus with finely dispersed chromatin and indistinct nucleoli, and a narrow rim of pale blue cytoplasm containing a small vacuole. Definite azurophilic granules and Auer rods are not seen in this cell. The morphology is that of a blast but does not by itself demonstrate the granular feature of granular ALL. Findings are compatible with a lymphoblast in the context of granular ALL; lineage must be confirmed by MPO cytochemistry and flow cytometry.

title: Marrow Germinal Center - 7.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at low power (apparently an immunohistochemical stain with weak brown chromogen; marker not labeled) shows hypercellular marrow containing several ill-defined lymphoid aggregates with faint granular staining concentrated within them. Megakaryocytes and other hematopoietic elements are present in the surrounding marrow. Well-formed germinal center architecture is not clearly appreciable in this image, and the weak signal limits interpretation. The findings are compatible with lymphoid aggregates corresponding to the reactive germinal centers shown in the H&E and CD20 images of this series.

title: Rituximab-Associated Marrow T-cell Hyperplasia - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy shows trabecular bone and cellular marrow with preserved trilineage hematopoiesis and megakaryocytes. A single interstitial, non-paratrabecular lymphoid aggregate composed of small lymphocytes with slightly ill-defined borders is present; no germinal center or paratrabecular extension is seen. H&E morphology alone cannot determine the lineage of the aggregate. In a patient treated with rituximab, immunostains showing a predominance of CD3+ T cells with absent CD20+ B cells would support rituximab-associated reactive T-cell aggregates rather than residual B-cell lymphoma.

title: Rituximab-Associated Marrow T-cell Hyperplasia - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at high power shows an interstitial collection of small lymphoid cells with round to slightly irregular hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm, admixed with scattered histiocytes, endothelial cells and small vessels. Cytologic atypia, large transformed cells and mitoses are not seen. Some small dark round nuclei could also represent erythroid precursors, so lineage assessment requires immunohistochemistry. In a post-rituximab setting, a CD3-positive, CD20/PAX5-negative infiltrate would be consistent with rituximab-associated marrow T-cell hyperplasia.

title: Myeloid Sarcoma -3
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of the dermal infiltrate shows sheets of monotonous medium-sized cells with oval nuclei and fine chromatin, the majority of which display weak-to-moderate, finely granular cytoplasmic and membranous staining; a rare cell stains strongly. The adjacent epidermis is negative. The specific antibody is not indicated in the image, so the stain must be interpreted alongside the rest of the panel. In context, diffuse positivity of the infiltrate with a myeloid-associated marker supports myeloid sarcoma.

title: AML with mutated CEBPA
describe_en: Low-power view of a bone marrow aspirate smear shows a hemodilute background with fat spaces and a markedly increased population of medium-to-large blasts occurring singly and in loose clusters. The blasts have high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, fine chromatin and scant basophilic cytoplasm; cytoplasmic granules and Auer rods cannot be evaluated at this magnification. Maturing myeloid and erythroid elements are sparse. Findings are consistent with acute myeloid leukemia; the CEBPA mutation status is a molecular finding and cannot be inferred from morphology.

title: Chronic Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows an enlarged neutrophil with a hypersegmented nucleus composed of multiple small lobes and cytoplasm with fine granules. Red cells show mild anisopoikilocytosis with a teardrop form, and platelets are present. No monocytes are included in this field, so the defining monocytosis cannot be evaluated here. Nuclear hypersegmentation may represent dysgranulopoiesis in a myeloid neoplasm such as chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, but megaloblastic change should be excluded.

title: Acute Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 2.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows several large blasts with high N:C ratios, round to slightly oval nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin and a thin rim of pale basophilic cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic granules and Auer rods are not seen, and definite monocytic features such as nuclear folding or gray vacuolated cytoplasm are not evident in these cells. The morphology indicates circulating blasts; separation of myeloblasts and monoblasts/promonocytes requires cytochemistry (MPO, NSE) and flow cytometry. These findings are compatible with, but not specific for, acute myelomonocytic leukemia.

title: Acute Myelomonocytic Leukemia - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows several large blasts with finely dispersed chromatin, indistinct nucleoli and scant to moderate basophilic cytoplasm without Auer rods. One blast has more abundant gray-blue cytoplasm, raising the possibility of monocytic differentiation, and a mature segmented neutrophil is present nearby. The monocytic and granulocytic components cannot be quantified from this field. Findings indicate circulating blasts and are compatible with acute myelomonocytic leukemia when supported by NSE/MPO cytochemistry and flow cytometry.

title: Accelerated Phase of CML - 2.
describe_en: The smear shows a cluster of granulocytic cells representing the full maturation spectrum, including one large blast with fine chromatin and basophilic cytoplasm, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands and segmented neutrophils. Obvious dysgranulopoiesis is not seen, and basophils are not clearly identified in this cluster. Accelerated phase criteria (blasts 10-19% or basophils >=20% in blood or marrow, or additional clonal abnormalities) cannot be assessed from a single field. The findings are compatible with CML showing a left-shifted granulocytic proliferation.

title: Accelerated Phase of CML - 4.
describe_en: The smear shows a prominent granulocytic population spanning myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands and segmented neutrophils, with several larger immature cells having finer chromatin and basophilic cytoplasm. Dysgranulopoiesis is not evident. Basophils are not clearly identified in this field, and the proportion of blasts cannot be established without a differential count. Findings are compatible with CML showing marked left shift; accelerated phase requires quantitative criteria.

title: Accelerated Phase of CML - 5.
describe_en: The preparation shows a small cluster of four nucleated cells. The largest has a bilobed nucleus and gray-blue, faintly granular cytoplasm, raising the possibility of a micromegakaryocyte, while two cells with irregular folded nuclei resemble immature granulocytes and one smaller cell with dense purple cytoplasm may be a basophil. Chromatin and granule detail are limited at this resolution, and cell lineage cannot be assigned with confidence without immunostaining (e.g., CD61) or a larger field. Such dysplastic megakaryocytes and basophils support, but do not by themselves establish, accelerated phase of CML.

title: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear, examined in a well-spread area, shows normocytic, normochromic red cells without significant anisopoikilocytosis. Platelets are markedly decreased, with essentially none present in this field, and no platelet clumping is identified to suggest pseudothrombocytopenia. Schistocytes are not seen, arguing against a microangiopathic process. No leukocytes are present in the field for assessment. Findings are consistent with isolated thrombocytopenia, as seen in immune thrombocytopenia, although the morphology is not specific.

title: Neuroblastoma Ganglion Cell Differentiation Following Chemotherapy - 1.
describe_en: Low-power view of a bone marrow core biopsy shows trabecular bone with intertrabecular spaces diffusely replaced by an infiltrate of dark cells arranged in streaming, fascicle-like patterns within pale fibrillary to fibrotic stroma. Normal fat and trilineage hematopoiesis are not appreciated. Individual cell morphology, including ganglion cell differentiation, cannot be assessed at this magnification. Findings are consistent with marrow involvement by treated metastatic neuroblastoma with stromal changes; higher-power examination is needed to document ganglion cell differentiation.

title: Neuroblastoma Ganglion Cell Differentiation Following Chemotherapy - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy shows trabecular bone with intertrabecular spaces diffusely replaced by small to intermediate-sized cells with round to oval hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. The cells stream within pale fibrillary to collagenous stroma, and normal hematopoietic elements are absent. Mature ganglion cells with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli are not identified in this field, so the degree of post-chemotherapy differentiation cannot be judged from this image alone. Findings are consistent with marrow involvement by metastatic neuroblastoma, with predominantly neuroblastic morphology in this field.

title: Neuroblastoma Ganglion Cell Differentiation Following Chemotherapy - 3.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at high power shows a loosely cohesive population of small to intermediate cells with oval to slightly spindled nuclei, fine chromatin, and scant cytoplasm, set within pale eosinophilic fibrillary stroma resembling neuropil. A subset of cells has slightly enlarged vesicular nuclei with small nucleoli, which may represent early differentiating neuroblasts, and occasional apoptotic nuclei are present. Mature ganglion cells with abundant cytoplasm are not seen in this field. Findings are consistent with metastatic neuroblastoma in the marrow, with at most early neuroblastic differentiation evident in this image.

title: Neuroblastoma Ganglion Cell Differentiation Following Chemotherapy - 4.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy shows, adjacent to a bony trabecula, a population of intermediate to large cells with oval to irregular nuclei, vesicular chromatin, small nucleoli, and moderate amounts of pale cytoplasm within pale fibrillary stroma. On the right, residual hematopoietic cells including erythroid precursors with small dense nuclei are present. The tumor cells are larger than undifferentiated neuroblasts, suggesting differentiating neuroblasts, but mature ganglion cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent single nucleoli are not clearly identified in this field. Findings are consistent with metastatic neuroblastoma with features of neuroblastic differentiation after therapy.

title: EBV-driven HIV-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma causing profound lactic acidosis
describe_en: Composite figure. Panel A (H&E) shows squamous epithelium with an underlying dermal infiltrate of atypical cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei among collagen bundles and small vessels. Panel B shows large atypical cells within adipose tissue with a strong dark nuclear signal, a pattern consistent with EBER in situ hybridization, although the stain is not labeled. Resolution and color balance limit detailed cytologic assessment, and the metabolic complication (lactic acidosis) cannot be evaluated morphologically. Findings are suggestive of an EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma in an HIV-positive patient, requiring CD20/PAX5, CD30, MUM1, Ki-67 and EBER studies for confirmation.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 1.
describe_en: Low-power peripheral blood smear shows a dense red cell monolayer with strikingly few leukocytes; only about five white cells are present, predominantly small mononuclear cells, and segmented neutrophils are essentially absent. Detailed cytology cannot be assessed at this magnification. Findings suggest severe neutropenia, compatible with severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann syndrome) in the appropriate clinical setting; an absolute neutrophil count is required for confirmation.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 10.
describe_en: Low-power immunohistochemical stain of a bone marrow core biopsy (antigen not specified) shows a cellular marrow with brown-positive cells scattered singly, in small clusters and in linear streaks among a predominantly negative population. Fat spaces are partly preserved and trabeculae are unremarkable. Interpretation depends on the antibody applied; in severe congenital neutropenia, such stains are used to demonstrate the distribution of myeloid precursors and the relative lack of mature neutrophils.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 11.
describe_en: Low-power immunohistochemical stain of a bone marrow core biopsy (antigen not specified) shows a hypercellular marrow in which numerous brown-positive cells are dispersed diffusely in an interstitial pattern among hematoxylin-counterstained negative cells. No sheets or aggregates of positive cells are seen. Interpretation depends on the antibody used; in severe congenital neutropenia, myeloid markers such as MPO typically highlight preserved early granulocytic precursors with a paucity of mature neutrophils.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 3.
describe_en: Low-power bone marrow aspirate smear is hemodilute, with small aggregates of nucleated cells along particle trails in a dense red cell background. The nucleated cells include medium-sized granulated precursors and small dark lymphocytes or erythroid precursors; mature segmented neutrophils are not readily apparent, but the magnification precludes reliable assessment. High-power evaluation is needed to document maturation arrest of granulopoiesis as seen in severe congenital neutropenia.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 6.
describe_en: Low-power bone marrow core biopsy shows markedly hypercellular marrow filling the spaces between anastomosing bony trabeculae, with few residual fat vacuoles and scattered megakaryocytes. Cytologic detail and myeloid maturation cannot be evaluated at this magnification. A hypercellular marrow is compatible with the myeloid hyperplasia and maturation arrest of severe congenital neutropenia but is nonspecific without higher-power and aspirate evaluation.

title: Kostmann's Syndrome - 7.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at intermediate power shows a hypercellular marrow with reduced fat. A dense, expanded zone of immature myeloid precursors with oval vesicular nuclei lies adjacent to a bony trabecula, with scattered eosinophils, erythroid islands and edematous hemorrhagic areas elsewhere. The proportion of mature neutrophils cannot be reliably assessed at this magnification. Findings suggest a left-shifted granulopoiesis compatible with severe congenital neutropenia, requiring aspirate differential for confirmation.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows red cells that are largely normocytic with scattered crenated forms (echinocytes), and very few platelets. A single small mature lymphocyte is the only leukocyte in the field, and no neutrophils are identified. No blasts or schistocytes are seen. Findings suggest leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, consistent with the cytopenias of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, although the peripheral smear itself is nonspecific.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 10.
describe_en: Low-power Prussian blue-stained bone marrow aspirate smear shows a particle containing abundant coarse, branching blue hemosiderin deposits within macrophages, indicating increased storage iron. Individual cells and hemophagocytosis cannot be evaluated at this magnification. Increased marrow iron stores are a nonspecific finding that can accompany hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with hyperferritinemia and inflammation-associated iron sequestration.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 11.
describe_en: Prussian blue-stained bone marrow aspirate smear shows a macrophage with abundant diffuse blue hemosiderin that appears to enclose several red-counterstained nuclei, suggestive of phagocytosed nucleated cells. Additional extracellular iron clumps are present nearby. Because the iron stain obscures cytoplasmic detail, true engulfment is best confirmed on a Wright-Giemsa smear. Findings are compatible with an iron-laden hemophagocytic macrophage as seen in hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 3.
describe_en: Low-power examination of a bone marrow aspirate smear shows a cellular specimen with a dense aggregate of hematopoietic cells and a smaller cluster near the feathered edge, along with scattered larger single cells in the cellular trails. Individual cell morphology, including the presence of phagocytosed blood cells within histiocytes, cannot be assessed at this magnification. The image is useful to locate particles and cellular areas where high-power search for hemophagocytic histiocytes should be performed. Diagnosis of hemophagocytic syndrome requires high-power confirmation and correlation with clinical and laboratory HLH criteria.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 7.
describe_en: Low-power bone marrow core biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with markedly reduced fat between thin bony trabeculae and areas of hemorrhage. Cellular detail, including histiocytes or hemophagocytosis, cannot be assessed at this magnification. The finding of a hypercellular marrow is nonspecific; evaluation for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis requires high-power review, CD163 immunostaining and aspirate correlation.

title: Hemophagocytic Syndrome - 9.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with a loose, edematous background and interstitial hemorrhage. Megakaryocytes, erythroid precursors and granulocytic cells are present, together with scattered histiocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, some of which appear to contain erythrocytes. Hemophagocytosis is difficult to confirm on H&E sections. Findings may be compatible with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in the appropriate context; CD163 immunostain and aspirate review are recommended.

title: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome - 10.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at low power shows a markedly hypercellular marrow with near-complete loss of fat spaces. The intertrabecular space is filled by a mixed hematopoietic population with patchy, looser eosinophilic areas and focal hemorrhage. Cytoplasmic giant granules cannot be assessed at this magnification. Findings are nonspecific; in the clinical context of Chediak-Higashi syndrome, a hypercellular marrow may reflect ineffective granulopoiesis or an accelerated (HLH-like) phase, to be confirmed on aspirate and high-power examination.

title: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome - 11.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at high power shows a hypercellular marrow with a mixed infiltrate. Many large cells have oval, folded or indented vesicular nuclei with small nucleoli and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, suggestive of histiocytes, admixed with erythroid precursors, eosinophils, lymphocytes and occasional mitoses in a hemorrhagic background. Cytoplasmic giant granules cannot be resolved on this section. In the context of Chediak-Higashi syndrome, the histiocyte-rich infiltrate raises concern for the accelerated (HLH-like) phase; CD163/CD68 IHC and aspirate correlation are recommended.

title: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome - 12.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at high power shows a hypercellular, hemorrhagic marrow with a prominent population of large histiocyte-like cells with oval vesicular nuclei and abundant pale cytoplasm, several of which appear to contain clustered erythrocytes. Eosinophils, lymphocytes and erythroid precursors are admixed. Giant cytoplasmic granules cannot be assessed on this section. In the setting of Chediak-Higashi syndrome, findings are suggestive of the accelerated phase with hemophagocytic histiocytic infiltration; CD163 immunostain and aspirate correlation are recommended.

title: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome - 3.
describe_en: Low-power view of a bone marrow aspirate smear shows a highly cellular particle composed of a mixed hematopoietic population with scattered megakaryocytes and few fat spaces. Cellular detail, including cytoplasmic granules, cannot be assessed at this magnification. The field documents adequate, cellular aspirate material; diagnostic giant granules of Chediak-Higashi syndrome require examination at high power.

title: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome - 6.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows two large macrophages. One contains cytoplasmic vacuoles with engulfed dense nuclear material and magenta particles, consistent with phagocytosis of cells or cell fragments; the other shows extensive cytoplasmic vacuolation. Surrounding granulocytic precursors show coarse granulation, but definitive giant granules are not clearly seen in this field. Findings are consistent with hemophagocytosis, as seen in the accelerated phase of Chediak-Higashi syndrome; confirmation of giant granules elsewhere on the smear is required.

title: Purple Bodies - 2.
describe_en: Smear shows a small cluster of immature myeloid-appearing cells in a background of red cells. Two large cells have eccentric nuclei, fine chromatin, a conspicuous paranuclear hof and basophilic cytoplasm lacking distinct granules, resembling hypogranular promyelocytes; two smaller cells with high N:C ratio and fine chromatin are also present. No mature neutrophils are seen in this field. The specific 'purple bodies' referenced in the title cannot be confidently identified in this image; findings are compatible with early myeloid precursors as seen in congenital neutropenia with maturation arrest, but correlation with the full aspirate is required.

title: Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome - 1.
describe_en: Low-power view of a bone marrow aspirate smear shows a particle composed predominantly of fat spaces and stromal elements with only sparse hematopoietic cells along its strands. Thick, dark areas with brown-black precipitate are present, and blood-diluted areas surround the particle. Cytologic detail, maturation, and dysplasia cannot be evaluated at this magnification. The overall impression is of a hypocellular particle, which in context is compatible with the marrow hypoplasia seen in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome; a core biopsy is needed for accurate cellularity assessment.

title: Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome - 2.
describe_en: High-power view of a bone marrow aspirate shows three early myeloid precursors with round to oval nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin and bluish cytoplasm containing fine purple granules that overlie the nucleus. No mature granulocytes are present in this field, and no Auer rods are identified. These appearances are non-specific; a myeloid maturation arrest-like or dysgranulopoietic pattern may be seen in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, but the diagnosis rests on neutropenia, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal findings and biallelic SBDS mutation. Findings are suggestive of, but not diagnostic for, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome in the appropriate clinical context.

title: Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome - 3.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at high power shows a stroma-rich fragment containing numerous fat vacuoles, spindle-shaped stromal cells, and fibrillar strands. Hematopoietic elements are sparse, consisting of a few granulated myeloid precursors and small lymphoid cells without obvious blast clusters. The composition suggests a hypocellular marrow with relative stromal prominence, which is compatible with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome in the appropriate clinical context. A single field cannot establish cellularity, and a trephine biopsy plus SBDS genetic testing are needed.

title: Breast Cancer - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows red cells with refractile drying artifact and two medium-sized mononuclear cells with round, slightly eccentric nuclei, moderately condensed chromatin and a moderate rim of pale blue agranular cytoplasm, next to a small lymphocyte and a small dark nuclear fragment. The cells are not clearly cohesive and lack definitive epithelial features. In a patient with breast cancer, these could represent circulating tumor cells (carcinocythemia), but reactive lymphocytes, monocytoid cells or plasmacytoid cells cannot be excluded; cytokeratin immunocytochemistry or flow cytometry is needed for confirmation.

title: Metastatic Prostatic Carcinoma - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows normochromic red cells with mild anisopoikilocytosis, including scattered teardrop cells and occasional fragmented, helmet-like forms. Platelets appear adequate. No leukocytes, nucleated red cells or circulating tumor cells are present in this field. These red cell changes are nonspecific; in a patient with metastatic prostatic carcinoma they are suggestive of marrow infiltration (myelophthisis) and/or tumor-associated microangiopathy or chronic DIC, but the carcinoma itself is not demonstrated in this image.

title: Hemoglobin S/HPFH - 3.
describe_en: High-power view of an acid-elution (Kleihauer-Betke) stained blood film taken from a thick area of the smear. Scattered red cells are intensely eosinophilic with slightly irregular outlines, set among a closely packed network of paler cell outlines that retain faint staining. The thickness of the field and the soft focus prevent reliable judgement of whether HbF is pancellular or heterocellular. In the context of the series, the image is presented as part of the HbS/HPFH evaluation, but interpretation should be based on a thin, well-spread area of the slide.

title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in leukemic phase with flower cell morphology
describe_en: Composite figure. The smear (A, Wright-Giemsa) shows a cluster of large atypical lymphoid cells with high N:C ratio, round to indented and notched nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, small nucleoli and basophilic, focally vacuolated cytoplasm, admixed with crenated red cells. Distinct multilobated flower-like nuclei are only subtly suggested by nuclear notching in this field. The tissue section (B) shows a diffuse infiltrate with strong nuclear immunostaining, antigen not specified. Findings are suggestive of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in leukemic phase, which should be confirmed by flow cytometry showing a clonal large B-cell population.

title: Hemoglobin S/HPFH - 4.
describe_en: Low-power view of a peripheral blood smear shows a well-spread monolayer of red cells of relatively uniform size and shape, with sparse leukocytes and platelets. No sickle cells, target cells or schistocytes are recognizable at this magnification, although fine morphologic detail cannot be assessed. The paucity of sickled forms is in keeping with compound heterozygosity for hemoglobin S and hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, in which pancellular HbF inhibits polymerization; the diagnosis requires hemoglobin HPLC/electrophoresis and HbF distribution studies rather than morphology.

title: Pleural Fluid Mast Cells - 1.
describe_en: Scanning-power view of a pleural fluid preparation shows a highly cellular specimen with numerous cohesive cell clusters of varying size and many dispersed single cells. At this magnification the individual cell types, including mast cells, cannot be identified, and nuclear features cannot be assessed. High-power examination and immunocytochemistry are needed to characterize the clusters as reactive mesothelial cells or metastatic tumor and to identify mast cells.

title: Howell-Jolly Bodies - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear at very high magnification shows a single nucleated cell with a round nucleus, coarsely clumped chromatin, and gray-lilac polychromatophilic cytoplasm, most consistent with a polychromatic normoblast. The cytoplasm contains several small, round, dense dark purple inclusions adjacent to the nucleus, resembling Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear fragments), along with small vacuoles. Classic Howell-Jolly bodies in mature anucleate red cells are not shown in this field. Findings are suggestive of Howell-Jolly body-like nuclear fragments in a nucleated red cell, as seen with dyserythropoiesis, megaloblastic change, or hyposplenism.

title: ad 1
describe_en: Composite figure. Tissue section (A) shows sheets of intermediate-sized mononuclear cells with oval to indented nuclei, fine chromatin and moderate pale cytoplasm. The peripheral blood smear (B) contains atypical mononuclear cells with irregular nuclei and grey-blue cytoplasm, and the bone marrow biopsy (C) is hypercellular with a diffuse mononuclear infiltrate; immunohistochemistry (D) highlights a focal cluster of positive cells, but the antigen is not identified. The title and category (acquired neutropenia) do not specify the diagnosis; the morphology is suggestive of a monocytic/histiocytoid neoplastic infiltrate involving tissue, blood and marrow, and definitive classification requires the immunophenotype.

title: ad 2
describe_en: Skin biopsy (H&E, low power) shows a dense, diffuse cellular infiltrate occupying the full thickness of the sampled dermis, dissecting between collagen bundles and extending up to the dermal-epidermal junction. The overlying epidermis is intact. Cytologic detail is not resolvable at this magnification, and the title and category do not specify a diagnosis. In a patient with acquired neutropenia, the pattern raises concern for a cutaneous hematolymphoid infiltrate such as leukemia cutis/myeloid sarcoma, which requires high-power review and immunohistochemistry (e.g., MPO, CD68, CD4, CD3, CD20) for classification.

title: Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma - 5.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a medium-to-large atypical lymphoid cell with a round, slightly indented nucleus, moderately condensed chromatin and a moderate rim of basophilic cytoplasm. The characteristic polylobated flower-like nucleus of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is not present in this cell. Red cells and platelets are unremarkable. Although ATLL may contain basophilic cells with less nuclear irregularity, this cell alone is not specific; the findings are compatible with ATLL only in conjunction with other flower cells, HTLV-1 serology and a CD4+ CD25+ CD7- T-cell phenotype.

title: APL in Niemann-Pick Disease - 2.
describe_en: Aspirate smear shows clusters of large abnormal promyelocytes with abundant cytoplasm densely packed with coarse azurophilic granules. Many nuclei are folded, reniform or bilobed, with fine chromatin partially obscured by granules. Rare small nucleated cells are present in the background, and no storage histiocytes are seen in this particular field. Findings are consistent with hypergranular acute promyelocytic leukemia; confirmation of PML::RARA is required and should be pursued urgently given coagulopathy risk.

title: Intravascular Large Cell Lymphoma - 1.
describe_en: Low-power view shows a fibrous wall lining a large empty lumen, with small intramural vessels that contain clusters of enlarged hyperchromatic cells admixed with erythrocytes. The surrounding collagenous stroma lacks a mass-forming or sheet-like infiltrate. Cytologic detail is limited at this magnification, so the atypia of the intravascular cells cannot be fully assessed. The distribution is suggestive of intravascular large B-cell lymphoma, best confirmed on higher power and with CD20 and CD34/CD31 immunostaining.

title: Intravascular Large Cell Lymphoma - 4.
describe_en: Tissue section shows a discrete aggregate of large atypical cells with vesicular nuclei, visible nucleoli and moderate amphophilic cytoplasm. The aggregate appears to lie within a vascular or sinusoidal space, surrounded by loose stroma rich in erythrocytes and mixed small cells. An endothelial lining around the aggregate is not clearly discernible at this magnification, so intravascular localization cannot be established on H&E alone. The findings are compatible with intravascular large B-cell lymphoma; CD20 and CD34/CD31 immunostains are needed to confirm an intraluminal B-cell population.

title: Intravascular Large Cell Lymphoma - 5.
describe_en: Tissue section shows loose, edematous stroma containing a mixed infiltrate of small lymphocytes and scattered large atypical cells with vesicular nuclei, irregular nuclear contours and prominent nucleoli. Thin-walled capillary channels and extravasated red cells are present. The large cells appear to lie in and around small vascular spaces, but a strictly intravascular distribution cannot be confirmed on this H&E field alone. The findings are compatible with involvement by intravascular large B-cell lymphoma in the appropriate context; CD20 with CD34 or CD31 immunostaining is recommended to demonstrate intraluminal localization.

title: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia - 3.
describe_en: Cellular smear shows a dense, monotonous population of lymphoid cells with round nuclei, moderately condensed chromatin and scant to moderate pale-blue cytoplasm. The arrow indicates a small lymphocyte with coarse, block-like chromatin typical of CLL. However, many cells in this field are somewhat larger than classic CLL cells, and some show small visible nucleoli, raising the possibility of increased prolymphocytes or thick-area artifact. The findings are compatible with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, but the prolymphocyte percentage should be enumerated and mantle cell lymphoma excluded by immunophenotyping.

title: Normal Plasma Cell Distribution Along Bone Marrow Sinusoid - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows a linear stromal-vascular fragment composed of elongated dark nuclei, along which numerous small round-nucleated cells are aligned. Some of the adjacent cells have moderate purple cytoplasm compatible with plasma cells, while scattered neutrophils, bands and erythroid precursors are present in the background. Heavy staining and cell overlap limit confident identification of individual plasma cells at this magnification. The pattern is compatible with the normal perivascular (perisinusoidal) distribution of marrow plasma cells; CD138 immunostaining on the core biopsy best demonstrates this arrangement.

title: Reactive Histiocytes in the Peripheral Blood - 1.
describe_en: Low-power view of a peripheral blood smear (thick area, with red cells aggregated into irregular clumps) shows several large mononuclear cells with round to oval nuclei and moderate amounts of pale gray-blue cytoplasm, one of which contains foamy cytoplasmic vacuoles. Small lymphocytes are interspersed and provide a size reference. At this magnification the cells are suggestive of circulating histiocytes/macrophages, but nuclear and cytoplasmic detail is insufficient to exclude monocytes, plasma cells, or other abnormal cells; high-power review (ideally of a buffy coat preparation) is required.

title: Hairy Cell Leukemia Variant - 5.
describe_en: Bone marrow biopsy section shows a hypercellular marrow with preserved megakaryocytes and eosinophilic precursors. Interspersed interstitially among hematopoietic elements is a population of mononuclear cells with round-to-oval nuclei, moderately open chromatin, occasional small nucleoli and moderate pale cytoplasm. The infiltrate is subtle and lacks the widely spaced fried-egg appearance of classic hairy cell leukemia, so its extent cannot be accurately estimated on H&E alone. Findings are compatible with interstitial involvement by hairy cell leukemia variant; CD20, CD79a/PAX5 and annexin A1 immunostains are recommended to highlight and characterize the infiltrate.

title: Anaplastic Large-Cell Lymphoma – Nodal Involvement - 1.
describe_en: Scanning-power view of a lymph node shows diffuse effacement of the normal architecture by pale-staining sheets of cells, with only a few small, dark-staining residual lymphoid follicles scattered throughout. Cytologic features cannot be evaluated at this magnification. The pattern indicates diffuse involvement by a neoplasm and is compatible with anaplastic large cell lymphoma in the appropriate context; higher-power evaluation for hallmark cells and immunohistochemistry for CD30, ALK, EMA and T-cell markers are required.

title: Anaplastic Large-Cell Lymphoma – Nodal Involvement - 7.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of a lymph node shows nuclear positivity in a large proportion of cells, predominantly large pleomorphic tumor nuclei, with variable intensity and a speckled pattern in some cells. Small background lymphocytes and stromal cells are largely negative, and there is no cytoplasmic or membranous staining. The antibody is not labeled; the purely nuclear pattern in a high fraction of tumor cells is most consistent with Ki-67, indicating a high proliferation index. Findings support a high-grade lymphoma, consistent with anaplastic large cell lymphoma in context.

title: Anaplastic Large-Cell Lymphoma – Nodal Involvement - 8.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of a lymph node at intermediate power shows a diffuse infiltrate of large atypical cells admixed with small lymphocytes. Many large cells show membranous ring-like positivity, while numerous background small lymphocytes are strongly positive and some large cells are weak or negative. The antibody is not labeled; the pattern indicates a lymphoid-lineage (T-cell or leukocyte) marker shared by tumor cells and reactive small lymphocytes. This supports a hematolymphoid origin of the large cells, consistent with anaplastic large cell lymphoma in context, but lineage assignment requires the full panel, because ALCL often loses pan-T-cell antigens such as CD3.

title: Megakaryocytic Hyperplasia - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at high power shows two large, mature megakaryocytes lying adjacent to each other, with multilobated overlapping nuclei and abundant finely granular cytoplasm. A small hematopoietic cell is present within the cytoplasm of one megakaryocyte, consistent with emperipolesis. The megakaryocytes lack obvious hypolobation, micro-forms or bizarre hyperchromatic nuclei in this field. Although two megakaryocytes in a single high-power field suggest increased numbers, megakaryocytic hyperplasia should be assessed by low-power evaluation of particles or the core biopsy; findings are compatible with megakaryocytic hyperplasia.

title: Look-alikes: ALL vs AMoL - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows large blasts with round to slightly reniform nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, small or inconspicuous nucleoli and abundant pale gray-blue cytoplasm containing fine vacuoles. Auer rods and cytoplasmic granules are not identified, and small mature lymphocytes are scattered in the background. The abundant cytoplasm and vacuolation mimic monoblasts, although the case is classified under precursor lymphoid neoplasms. Morphology cannot assign lineage here; flow cytometry, TdT and nonspecific esterase/MPO cytochemistry are needed to distinguish B-lymphoblastic leukemia from acute monoblastic leukemia.

title: LE cell in joint fluid - 1.
describe_en: Low-power cytospin of synovial fluid shows an inflammatory cell population composed of numerous neutrophils and lymphocytes with scattered vacuolated macrophages. A few round, homogeneous pink-purple bodies are present in the background and near phagocytes. At this magnification, LE cells (neutrophils containing a phagocytosed homogeneous nuclear mass) cannot be confidently identified, and higher-power examination is required. Findings are consistent with an inflammatory synovial effusion, and the homogeneous bodies raise the possibility of LE phenomenon in a patient with lupus.

title: RBC aggluntination - 3.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows predominantly dispersed normocytic red cells with scattered small, irregular aggregates of two to five overlapping erythrocytes, without linear rouleaux formation. A mature lymphocyte and scattered platelets are present. No definite spherocytes are identified in this field. The findings are suggestive of mild red cell agglutination; because the degree is subtle, correlation with warming of the sample, a direct antiglobulin test, and cold agglutinin titer is advised.

title: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, unspecified bone marrow aspirate - 1.
describe_en: Low-power view of the bone marrow aspirate smear shows a cellular specimen with trilineage hematopoiesis, including maturing granulocytic and erythroid elements and occasional eosinophils. Scattered medium to large mononuclear cells with irregular nuclear contours are present, which may represent atypical lymphoid cells, but they cannot be confidently distinguished from normal precursors at this magnification. Morphology alone is insufficient; correlation with the trephine biopsy, immunohistochemistry, and flow cytometry is needed to document involvement by peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS.

title: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, unspecified bone marrow aspirate - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at high power shows abundant maturing granulocytic elements with orderly progression to segmented neutrophils, along with erythroid precursors and an occasional eosinophil. Admixed are small to medium mononuclear cells with coarse chromatin and mildly irregular nuclear contours, which may represent atypical T cells, although they are not morphologically distinctive. Correlation with trephine biopsy immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies is required to establish involvement by peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS.

title: Look-alikes: Hematopoietic cluster vs. extrinsic cells - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows a dense, thick cluster of overlapping cells with molded borders, surrounded by dispersed red cells and hematopoietic elements. Cells at the edge of the cluster have granular cytoplasm resembling granulocytic precursors and appear to merge with the surrounding marrow cells, favoring a clump of hematopoietic cells. Nuclear detail in the center is obscured by thickness, so a cohesive extrinsic (metastatic) cell cluster cannot be fully excluded on this image alone. Examination of the cluster edge at higher power, the trephine biopsy, and immunostains (e.g., keratin) are recommended if concern persists.

title: May-Hegglin anomoly - 5.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows normocytic, normochromic red cells with few platelets in the field. A giant platelet approaching red-cell size is present adjacent to an unremarkable eosinophil, with a normal-sized platelet nearby. No neutrophils are present in this field, so the characteristic basophilic Döhle-like cytoplasmic inclusions cannot be evaluated here. In the appropriate context, macrothrombocytopenia is suggestive of an MYH9-related disorder (May-Hegglin anomaly).

title: Dysgranulopoiesis - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear shows a cellular, crowded particle edge composed predominantly of granulocytic precursors. Many myelocytes, metamyelocytes and band forms have pale, hypogranular cytoplasm, and some mature forms show round to hyposegmented nuclei. Larger immature cells with finer chromatin are also present, although blasts cannot be reliably enumerated in this thick field. The overlapping cells and thick smear limit assessment of individual dysplastic features. Findings are suggestive of dysgranulopoiesis with hypogranularity; confirmation in thinner areas with a formal count is recommended.

title: Dysgranulopoiesis - 6.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a neutrophil with a C-shaped, non-segmented nucleus containing coarsely clumped, mature-appearing chromatin, a nuclear-maturation mismatch suggestive of hyposegmentation. The cytoplasm contains relatively coarse granules, and hypogranularity is not evident. The surrounding red cells and platelet are unremarkable. In isolation this cell could represent a normal band form; hyposegmented neutrophils with clumped chromatin, when numerous (at least 10% of neutrophils), support dysgranulopoiesis as seen in myelodysplastic neoplasms.

title: Dysgranulopoiesis - 8.
describe_en: Smear (likely bone marrow aspirate) shows a large cell with gray-blue, essentially agranular cytoplasm containing numerous round, dense nuclear fragments of variable size, accompanied by several immature myeloid cells. Red cells show drying artifact with refractile holes and crenation. In the context of dysgranulopoiesis, the cell is interpreted as a dysplastic granulocytic precursor with nuclear fragmentation and hypogranularity. However, a single fragmented cell is not specific, and an apoptotic cell or a macrophage containing ingested nuclear debris cannot be excluded without evaluating additional fields.

title: Döhle body inclusions - 4.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows an eosinophil with a bilobed nucleus and abundant coarse orange-red granules. A small, pale blue, relatively granule-poor cytoplasmic area adjacent to the nucleus may represent a Döhle body, but it is not clearly separable from normal cytoplasm between granules. No neutrophil with a definite Döhle body is present in this field, so the image only partially illustrates the title. A large platelet and unremarkable red cells are also seen. Findings show an eosinophil with a possible Döhle-like cytoplasmic inclusion; Döhle bodies are best assessed in neutrophils.

title: Recurrent AML following peripheral stem cell transplant - 3.
describe_en: Section at intermediate power shows a diffuse, sheet-like infiltrate of medium-to-large cells with ovoid to spindled nuclei, fine chromatin, and scant cytoplasm arranged in a vaguely streaming pattern. There is moderate pleomorphism with scattered large hyperchromatic cells and mitoses, and no residual normal architecture is seen. The morphology is not lineage-specific. In the clinical context of recurrent AML after stem cell transplant, findings are suggestive of leukemic infiltration (myeloid sarcoma), to be confirmed by immunohistochemistry for CD34, CD117, MPO, CD68/lysozyme, and exclusion of carcinoma, melanoma, and sarcoma.

title: Recurrent AML following peripheral stem cell transplant - 7.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of a bone marrow trephine biopsy shows a large, sheet-like infiltrate of monotonous medium-sized cells that are negative for the applied marker, effacing normal marrow architecture adjacent to a bony trabecula. A band of residual small immunopositive cells is present at the lower left, with only scattered positive cells within the infiltrate. The antigen is not specified; if this represents a maturing myeloid or lineage marker (e.g., MPO or CD3), the pattern indicates replacement of residual hematopoiesis by a negative neoplastic population. In the clinical setting of prior stem cell transplant, the findings are consistent with recurrent acute myeloid leukemia, to be confirmed with CD34/CD117 immunostains, flow cytometry, and chimerism studies.

title: Recurrent AML following peripheral stem cell transplant - 8.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain on a tissue section shows dense sheets of medium-sized cells with strong membranous and cytoplasmic staining in a diffuse infiltrative pattern, with a less cellular, largely negative area in the lower left containing scattered positive cells. The antibody and the anatomic site are not indicated in the image, so lineage cannot be assigned from this figure alone. In the context of recurrent acute myeloid leukemia after peripheral stem cell transplantation, the findings are suggestive of an infiltrate of recurrent leukemia (e.g., marrow relapse or myeloid sarcoma); correlation with a myeloid panel (CD34, CD117, MPO, CD33, CD43, lysozyme) and chimerism studies is required.

title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, T-cell/histiocyte rich variant - lymph node - 5.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain on a lymph node section shows membranous staining of numerous dispersed intermediate-to-large cells, set against a background of negative small lymphocytes. The positive cells are distributed singly and in small loose groups without forming sheets. Because the antibody is not labeled, the precise interpretation is limited: in T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma, CD20 or PAX5 would highlight the scattered large neoplastic B cells, whereas CD3 would highlight the predominant background T cells. Findings should be interpreted together with the H&E and the full immunohistochemical panel.

title: Bone marrow involvement in Niemann Pick disease - 5.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at low power shows a cellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis between bony trabeculae. Scattered pale, clear to finely vacuolated foci consistent with clusters of foamy histiocytes are present, along with focal aggregates of brown granular pigment. Individual cell detail is limited at this magnification. In the clinical context, findings are consistent with marrow involvement by a lipid storage disorder such as Niemann-Pick disease; higher-power examination and aspirate smears are needed to characterize the storage cells.

title: Bone marrow involvement in Niemann Pick disease - 6.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy section shows a hypercellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis. Interspersed among the hematopoietic elements are scattered large histiocytes with abundant pale, lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cytoplasmic vacuolation is not clearly resolved at this power, and no discrete sheets or granulomas are seen. In the context of the aspirate findings, the pale histiocytes are consistent with marrow involvement by Niemann-Pick disease; correlation with aspirate smears and enzymatic/genetic testing is required.

title: HIV-related plasmacytosis - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy at low power shows a markedly hypercellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis, numerous dispersed megakaryocytes, and focal streaming stromal bands. Scattered hemosiderin deposits are present. Plasma cells cannot be reliably identified or quantified at this magnification. The overall picture is that of a hypercellular reactive marrow, which in the HIV setting commonly accompanies polyclonal plasmacytosis; higher-power evaluation with CD138 and kappa/lambda stains is required.

title: HIV-related plasmacytosis - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow core biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and numerous megakaryocytes. Scattered plasma cells with eccentric nuclei and amphophilic cytoplasm are present interstitially, but they do not form clusters or sheets and are difficult to quantify at this magnification. Focal hemosiderin-laden macrophages are noted. The findings are compatible with a reactive marrow with interstitial plasmacytosis in the setting of HIV infection; CD138 and kappa/lambda immunostains are needed to quantify plasma cells and confirm polytypism.

title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma - bone marrow aspirate - 3.
describe_en: Smear from the stated bone marrow aspirate shows a blood-rich field with only rare nucleated cells, including a large atypical mononuclear cell (arrow) with a high N:C ratio, finely granular chromatin and a moderate rim of agranular blue cytoplasm. A smaller mononuclear cell at the upper right provides size comparison. Hematopoietic precursors are sparse, so this field is hemodiluted and resembles peripheral blood. A single atypical large cell is suggestive of but not diagnostic for involvement by large B-cell lymphoma; evaluation of cellular particles, flow cytometry and core biopsy are required.

title: Bone marrow granulomas secondary to Histoplasmosis sepsis - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a band neutrophil with vacuolated cytoplasm containing several small, oval yeast-like organisms with clear halos (arrow), adjacent to a vacuolated monocyte and a dense dark overlying body. Another neutrophil shows toxic granulation, and red cells are crenated. Although titled as a marrow granuloma case, this image is a blood smear. Findings are consistent with intracellular Histoplasma capsulatum in circulating neutrophils, indicating disseminated histoplasmosis with a high organism burden.

title: Bone marrow granulomas secondary to Histoplasmosis sepsis - 10.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain (antigen not specified) on a hypercellular bone marrow core shows scattered positive small round cells with crisp ring-like membranous staining among negative hematopoietic elements. A central, loosely arranged area of pale oval epithelioid-appearing nuclei, suggestive of a granuloma, contains a small aggregate of positive cells at its periphery and within it. Because the marker is not stated, the positive cells cannot be definitively assigned to a lineage, and fungal organisms are not assessable on this preparation. The appearance is compatible with a lymphocyte subset accompanying a marrow granuloma in disseminated histoplasmosis; GMS or PAS stains and culture are required to demonstrate Histoplasma.

title: Bone marrow granulomas secondary to Histoplasmosis sepsis - 2.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows a segmented neutrophil containing several small, oval, intracytoplasmic yeast-like organisms (arrow) measuring approximately 2–4 µm, each with a clear surrounding halo and an eccentric crescent of basophilic material; no kinetoplast is seen. An adjacent neutrophil shows toxic-appearing granulation, and red cells are crenated. Although titled as a marrow granuloma case, this image is a blood smear. Findings are consistent with circulating intracellular Histoplasma capsulatum in disseminated histoplasmosis, to be confirmed by culture and antigen testing.

title: Bone marrow granulomas secondary to Histoplasmosis sepsis - 9.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of the bone marrow biopsy shows numerous scattered cells with granular brown cytoplasmic staining and irregular, dendritic-like processes distributed interstitially throughout the marrow, with a vague central concentration. The specific antibody is not indicated, but the staining pattern is consistent with a histiocytic marker such as CD68 or CD163. A compact granuloma is not delineated in this field, and organisms cannot be assessed on this stain. Findings indicate an increased interstitial histiocytic population, compatible with the loose granulomatous response of disseminated histoplasmosis.

title: Cytogram- Hyperleukocytosis in AML - 3.
describe_en: Although titled as a cytogram, this image is a low-power peripheral blood smear rather than an automated analyzer plot. It shows striking leukocytosis composed of a monotonous population of medium to large blasts with high N:C ratio, round nuclei and scant pale-blue cytoplasm; nucleoli, granules and Auer rods cannot be assessed at this magnification. Mature leukocytes are rare. Findings are consistent with hyperleukocytosis due to acute leukemia, in keeping with the stated AML; the high blast count predisposes to leukostasis and can interfere with automated counts.

title: Cytogram- Hyperleukocytosis in AML - 4.
describe_en: Although titled as a cytogram, this image is a peripheral blood smear rather than an analyzer scatterplot. It shows a marked increase in large blasts with high N:C ratio, round to indented nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, occasional small nucleoli and a moderate rim of pale-blue, largely agranular cytoplasm; Auer rods are not seen in this field. Normal leukocytes are rare. Findings are consistent with the blood picture of hyperleukocytosis in acute myeloid leukemia, with lineage assignment requiring cytochemistry (MPO) and flow cytometry.

title: Leukemia cutis - 3
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear is hypercellular and nearly replaced by large blasts with abundant grey-blue, moderately basophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, delicate lacy chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Auer rods are not seen, and residual granulocytic and erythroid elements are markedly reduced. Although titled leukemia cutis, this image depicts the marrow rather than the skin lesion. Findings are consistent with acute monoblastic leukemia; nonspecific esterase cytochemistry and flow cytometry (CD14, CD64, CD11b, CD4) are recommended for confirmation.

title: Relapsed precursor B-ALL–bone marrow biopsy - 1.
describe_en: Low-power bone marrow core biopsy shows trabecular bone with intertrabecular marrow of moderate cellularity. The hematopoietic space is diffusely populated by a monotonous infiltrate of small, dark, round nuclei with loss of the normal mixed trilineage pattern, and megakaryocytes are markedly reduced. Cytologic detail is not assessable at this power. In a patient with prior precursor B-lymphoblastic leukemia, the findings are consistent with relapsed disease, pending higher-power review and TdT, CD34, CD19 and PAX5 immunostains or flow cytometry.

title: GVHD–bone marrow aspirate - 1.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at low power shows marrow particles composed predominantly of adipocytes and stromal strands, with markedly reduced hematopoietic elements. Small mononuclear cells are scattered along the stroma, and the background is paucicellular. Cytologic detail cannot be assessed at this magnification. Findings indicate a hypocellular marrow, which in a transplant recipient with chronic graft-versus-host disease may reflect immune-mediated marrow failure; graft failure, relapse, viral infection and drug effect should be excluded.

title: GVHD–bone marrow aspirate - 2.
describe_en: Bone marrow aspirate smear at higher power shows a particle composed largely of stromal cells with oval to spindled nuclei, hemosiderin-laden macrophages and fat vacuoles. Hematopoietic cells are sparse, limited to occasional neutrophils and small mononuclear cells, with no identifiable erythroid precursors or megakaryocytes in this field. No blasts or viral inclusions are seen. Findings are consistent with a hypocellular, stroma-rich marrow with increased storage iron; these changes are nonspecific but compatible with marrow hypoplasia in the setting of chronic graft-versus-host disease.

title: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis associated with AML-M5a - 1.
describe_en: Peripheral blood smear shows several large monocytic cells with round to folded nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm with irregular, blebbed borders. The fine chromatin suggests immature monocytic forms, although nucleoli are not well resolved at this magnification. Hemophagocytosis is not seen in this field, so the HLH component of the title cannot be confirmed from this image. Findings are suggestive of circulating immature monocytic cells, compatible with acute monocytic leukemia; blast enumeration, cytochemistry (nonspecific esterase) and flow cytometry are needed.

title: Systemic mastocytosis - 5.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain (DAB; marker not specified) on a bone marrow biopsy shows a cluster and scattered individual small round cells with strong membranous positivity at the periphery of a pale, spindle-cell-rich lesion; the spindle cells within the lesion are negative. Because the marker is not stated and the positive cells are round rather than spindled, this stain may highlight an accompanying lymphoid component of a mastocytosis lesion rather than the mast cells themselves. Interpretation for systemic mastocytosis requires correlation with tryptase, CD117 and CD25 stains.

title: Systemic mastocytosis - 6.
describe_en: Low-power immunohistochemical stain (DAB; marker not specified) of a hypercellular bone marrow biopsy shows scattered positive cells distributed singly and in small loose clusters throughout the interstitium. No compact multifocal aggregates are identified in this field. If this represents a mast cell marker, an interstitial increase of mast cells alone does not meet the WHO major criterion, and minor criteria (spindled morphology >25%, CD25/CD2/CD30 aberrancy, KIT D816V, serum tryptase >20 ng/mL) must be evaluated. Findings are suggestive of, but not by themselves diagnostic of, marrow involvement by systemic mastocytosis.

title: Systemic mastocytosis - 7.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain on a bone marrow biopsy (DAB; marker not specified, likely a mast cell marker such as tryptase or CD117) highlights a large, dense, compact aggregate of positive cells, with additional scattered spindle-shaped positive cells in the interstitium. The remaining hematopoietic elements are negative. A compact aggregate of more than 15 mast cells fulfills the major WHO criterion; findings are consistent with bone marrow involvement by systemic mastocytosis, with CD25/CD2 aberrancy and KIT D816V testing recommended for confirmation.

title: T-prolymphocytic leukemia cutis - 4.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain (red chromogen; specific marker not indicated) on a skin biopsy shows a dense dermal lymphoid infiltrate with diffuse, strong membranous positivity in nearly all neoplastic cells. The infiltrate surrounds and cuffs a negative adnexal epithelial structure and perivascular spaces. Cytologic detail is limited on this immunostain. In the context of a known T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia, the diffuse positivity for a T-cell antigen is consistent with cutaneous involvement (leukemia cutis); TCL1 expression would support the diagnosis.

title: T-prolymphocytic leukemia cutis - 5.
describe_en: Immunohistochemical stain of a skin biopsy (antibody not specified) shows dense perivascular and periadnexal dermal aggregates of small-to-medium lymphoid cells that are essentially negative for the marker, with only hematoxylin counterstain visible. The infiltrate extends into the superficial dermis up to the dermoepidermal junction. The image documents a negative immunostain in the dermal infiltrate; its significance depends on the antibody used (for example, CD8, CD25 or a B-cell marker would be expected to be negative in T-prolymphocytic leukemia cutis).

title: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma, Anaplastic Variant - 1.
describe_en: H&E section at intermediate power shows diffuse effacement by sheets of cohesive medium-to-large atypical cells with moderate pale to clear cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei with vesicular chromatin and small nucleoli, separated by delicate collagenous and vascular strands. Scattered mitotic figures are seen, and residual small lymphocytes are present at the periphery. Marked nuclear pleomorphism is not well appreciated at this magnification. Findings are consistent with a large cell lymphoma with a cohesive growth pattern; immunohistochemistry (CD20, PAX5, CD30, ALK, CD3, keratin) is needed to establish the anaplastic variant of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and exclude ALCL and carcinoma.

title: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma, Anaplastic Variant - 2.
